transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-09-18
Start: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Sanjay (AstraCompute Partnerships), Lena (AstraCompute Product), Tom (AstraCompute Infra)

Summary (auto-gen, imperfect):
Intro to potential partnership, discuss GPU fleet integration and co-sell, initial pilot ideas, security questions around KMS, VPC peering and audit logs. Agreed to share benchmarks and schedule a technical deep-dive.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Maya (Redwood): Hey, everyone. Thanks for joining, appreciate you taking the time. Uh, quick round of intros? I'll kick off, I'm Maya, AE at Redwood, and with me is Diego, our SE who runs infra and benchmarks.
[00:12] Diego (Redwood): Hi all, Diego here, happy to dig into perf and network details.
[00:17] Sanjay (AstraCompute): Sanjay, partnerships. Thanks for reaching out. We talked a bit over email.
[00:21] Lena (AstraCompute): Lena, Head of Product. Looking forward to hearing how we might integrate.
[00:25] Tom (AstraCompute): Tom, infra. I'll be focused on operational constraints and connectivity.
[00:29] Maya: Great. Goal today is quick intro, high-level partner models (is it marketplace, resell, infra integration), and then surface technical blockers. We can follow up with a deeper SE session for tests. Sound good?
[00:40] Sanjay: Sounds good. We're exploring partnerships with GPU fleet providers and infra partners. We have some customers asking for lower latency on inference and more flexible cost models, so this could fit.
[00:50] Lena: Also want to understand the flow for private deployments - VPCs, on-prem options, and data protections.
[00:57] Maya: Sure. High-level from Redwood: we offer hosted API, dedicated reserved capacity, and private deployments with VPC/on-prem options. We focus on predictable latency and observability. For partners, we've done both close integrations (peering with dedicated GPU pools) and marketplace-style referrals.
[01:12] Tom: When you say peering, are we talking VPC peering, private links? What's the network pattern?
[01:18] Diego: Typically we support VPC peering and private links; for dedicated capacity we can colocate in partner accounts or in our environment with private connectivity. There's some variation based on partner preference and compliance needs.
[01:30] Sanjay: Ok, a few things we care about: 1) How do you route requests to partner GPUs vs Redwood clusters? 2) Is there an autoscale/burst model? 3) What about billing split and attribution for co-sell?
[01:44] Maya: Great questions. Routing can be policy-based - latency-first, cost-first, region. For partner integrations we usually surface it as a model variant in the catalog and routing rules map customer requests to the variant which hits partner capacity. Autoscale and burst are supported on Dedicated with configurable policies. Billing splits are usually handled via partner contracts; we can export per-request usage and token-level cost breakdowns for attribution.
[02:05] Lena: How much ops overhead on your side? If we want to expose our fleet as 'AstraGPU-v1' in your catalog, how long to onboard?
[02:13] Diego: Onboarding time depends on whether it's API-level integration or private deployment. API integration with dedicated pools might take 2-4 weeks for initial validation; a private deployment in customer's VPC can take longer due to networking/security and compliance checks.
[02:24] Tom: On private deployments, we need to validate KMS integration, audit logs, and SSO. You mentioned audit logs - what granularity do you provide?
[02:32] Maya: We capture token-level cost and latency breakdowns, per-route/model dashboards, and have audit hooks. For enterprise we support KMS/HSM integrations and SSO/SAML, plus RBAC. We can share SOC 2 and other security docs.
[02:45] Sanjay: Awesome. Can you share a sample security checklist we can give to our compliance folks?
[02:49] Maya: Yes, we'll include our security overview in the follow up.
[02:52] [00:03:00] Diego: To start thinking about benchmarks, can you share two representative workloads? For example, a chat workload with context length ~2k tokens and a completion workload with short prompts but high qps.
[03:12] Tom: Yeah, we can provide QPS numbers and typical prompt sizes. We run both long-form summarization and short classification pipelines.
[03:20] Lena: Some customers also want embeddings batches; is that supported?
[03:24] Diego: Yes, embeddings and reranking are supported. For embeddings batching can drastically reduce unit cost. We'll propose quantization profiles too if that helps.
[03:31] Sanjay: On the hardware side, what GPU types are you optimized for? We run mixed fleets - some A100s, some H100s, and some Ampere variants.
[03:40] Maya: Our runtime supports a range; kernel selection is automatic and we optimize based on model architecture and sequence length distribution. For certain optimizations we might recommend specific GPU types or quantization.
[03:50] Sanjay: Any concerns about model compatibility? We run a few open LLMs and a custom fine-tuned model.
[03:57] Diego: We onboard open models often; for custom models we validate the model artifacts and run a small compatibility test. KV cache handling and attention optimizations are common sticking points but usually resolvable.
[04:10] [00:05:00] Tom: Network - what's the expected egress and do you require direct peering? We prefer minimizing cross-cloud egress charges.
[04:18] Maya: We can support in-region partner capacity to avoid cross-cloud egress. Direct peering or private link reduces latency and egress. We'll work with infra to figure cost-efficient topology.
[04:28] Lena: Are you able to run on our private infra if needed, like a customer-managed on-prem?
[04:33] Maya: Yes, we have Private deployments and on-prem packages for regulated workloads. That typically involves more ops work and a customer-managed control plane option.
[04:40] Sanjay: Pricing thoughts - for pilots do you have a standard commercial model? Flat credits, revenue share, or pay-as-you-go?
[04:48] Maya: We do usage-based hosted pricing, reserved capacity for Dedicated, and enterprise licensing for Private. For partners we often do pilot credits or discounted reserved capacity, then move to a revenue share or referral arrangement based on deal sizes.
[04:59] [00:07:00] Diego: From a technical POV, for benchmarking we'll want a network path, sample payloads, and ideally a test account with partner capacity exposed. That lets us measure p95 and throughput.
[05:14] Tom: We'll provision a test account; I need to sync with ops about who can create service endpoints.
[05:20] Sanjay: We'll also want a short partner MOU to outline pilot scope.
[05:24] Maya: Agreed. We'll draft a short one-pager and include responsibilities.
[05:28] [00:09:00] Lena: On security again, for audits we might need encryption in transit and at rest - is that default?
[05:36] Diego: Encryption in transit is standard. At rest depends on deployment: hosted uses our managed keys unless customer provides KMS; private/on-prem supports customer-managed KMS.
[05:45] Sanjay: Any regulatory red flags for EU customers? Data residency?
[05:49] Maya: We support regional deployments and can pin model versions and storage to regions to comply with data residency. We'll flag any latency tradeoffs.
[05:58] [00:11:00] Tom: Operationally, what are typical SLAs for Dedicated?
[06:03] Maya: SLA options exist for Dedicated capacity - uptime and latency targets are configurable depending on the commitment level. We can share our SLA docs.
[06:10] Diego: Also worth noting we have automatic fallback policies - if partner capacity is constrained, we can route to a compatible model variant to preserve availability.
[06:21] Sanjay: That fallback is helpful. What about observability for partners - can we see per-customer usage?
[06:27] Maya: Yes, we surface per-route/model dashboards and token-level traces. For partner integrations we can provide an aggregated view or shared dashboards depending on the agreement.
[06:38] [00:13:00] Lena: One nit - some of our customers require SOC2 + ISO27001. Do you have those?
[06:44] Maya: We have SOC 2 Type II and are working on ISO. We'll attach the compliance pack in the follow-up.
[06:50] [overlap] Tom: Great.
[06:52] [00:14:00] Sanjay: Thinking about next steps - pilot, benchmarks, legal MOU, then technical deep-dive. Anything else?
[06:59] Maya: That's perfect. We'll send the partner deck, security overview, and a benchmark spreadsheet. Diego will propose a test config. Can we target the deep-dive next week?
[07:10] Tom: Next week works; mornings are better for us PST.
[07:14] Lena: Same here.
[07:15] Sanjay: I'll coordinate schedules and loop in legal once we have the MOU.
[07:19] Diego: I'll prep an initial perf plan and example load generator suggestions.
[07:23] Maya: Cool. Any final questions or blockers we should call out now?
[07:28] Lena: Not from product side. Just need the security docs for legal.
[07:32] Tom: We'll gather the workload samples and infra specs.
[07:35] Sanjay: Ok, thanks everyone.
[07:37] Maya: Thanks all - we'll follow up with the docs and schedule.
[07:41] [00:16:00] (meeting ends, recorded length 48:02)

References/links mentioned: Redwood partner deck (link to be shared), security pack (SOC2), benchmark spreadsheet (to be shared).

Notes on transcription fidelity: transcription has occasional mis-hearings (e.g., "K V cash" for KV cache), names spelled inconsistently. Speaker turns approximate.
